title: breath of death vii
text: Breath of Death VII is an old school RPG where you find your party members and fight random battles with a turn based system. Part of the charm to this game is that it mimics the original Dragon Quest games in color, menus, maps and even the feel of the towns. After each battle, each party member gets restored to full health, including dead characters. Even if you escape, you get full health. This makes the game streamlined and easy even on hard difficulty. To compensate for this, the game balances out by powering up the monsters after each round. Their attack strength keep going up by 10%. It puts pressure to finish the fight fast. There is also no run, but instead its relegated to a magic skill given to one character. One of the biggest enjoyments that I get out of the game is the ability to chose one of two bonuses every time a character reaches a new level. Do you chose this spell or that spell? Do you want +20 Max HP and +20 strength or +10 Strength + 10 Willpower +10 Magic +10 Vitality? After level 30, the game runs out of choices for you. The challenge is in your MP / mana. You will get some back after each level, but outside of an Inn or a save point (you can save on the fly too). You won't be able to refill your magic. On the surface, fighting and button mashing make quick work of enemies. Deeper into any dungeon makes fighting difficult without using magic or techniques (both cost MP / mana). While battles are random, the dungeons have specific numbers of battles before the random battles get down to 0. So if you fight 20 random battles, you won't have any other random battles to fight. This works well, because you can go deep into a dungeon, have no mana left and need to walk back out of the dungeon. Having 0 remaining random battles ensures your survival. Since there is no sort of easy teleportation. A few dungeons force you to beat the boss and walk back. Luckily there is a run button. Spells get upgraded. The heal spell can get upgraded to resurrect. Making it easy if a character dies that you're trying to heal, well they're just resurrected! There aren't items, but there are potions. You can't buy these, you need to find them in caves. They resurrect and give full health to any character. These are necessary if your lone healer dies. There is a health regenerating zombie though and a vampire sort of attack with another character. The leader of your party is a silent (yet thinking) skeleton, a ghost princess healer, a vampire nerd and a prince zombie. They are all powerful in their own way. In battle, two of the characters can join forces for big attacks. The only problem is both need to be alive to do them. Its not a problem toward the beginning of the game. About 7 hours into the game, I noticed there is a combo system. Sure its always been there. I just didn't find it useful. Every attack builds a combo. There are special combo boosts and breakers that when used will multiply the damage by the combo, but reset the combo to 0. It would be more useful if these specials weren't already the highest damagers in general. You can keep using them to kill the enemies quickly without having to build a combo. When I played, I found normal (medium) difficulty far too easy, so I played on hard. On hard, the bosses became insurmountable. Like any RPG, grinding made any boss easier. The menu has a 'fight' command that will cue up a random battle for you! For the most part random battles are a numbers game. Not your stats vs their stats, but your remaining members against their remaining members. The party that outnumbers the other wins unless one of them balances out the numbers. Bosses were a major issue on hard, which made for an hour long grind on many of them. One boss, I had literally run out of enemies to grind and couldn't beat a boss. I had to leave the dungeon by walking mind you and grind on over world enemies. Then walk all the way back to the boss with 0 enemies. It just felt unnecessary and hindered my ability to enjoy the game. For equipment, Breath of Death is bare bones. You have a weapon and armor. No headgear, no accessory. Towns don't have more than a couple weapons and armor for your four characters. There are a few treasures here and there in dungeons. Treasures in towns get relegated to jokes, like "A true hero wouldn't steal from a person, even if there's a bazooka in there." There is no interaction with anything outside of talking to townspeople. Nothing hidden in book shelves or pots. It is sad how little effort got put into the details outside of readable tombstones in one lone graveyard. The world itself feels big enough. There are around 10+ dungeons and 3+ towns. You won't get to travel the oceans or visit far off lands, but the dungeons are the real maps. Each dungeon feels big enough. There are mostly underground areas, a prison and the ruins of giant towns. You can tackle them pretty openly. The second area has three dungeons you can visit. Yet, with the fourth, it bluntly tells you not to go in there yet. It just seems like a cheap reason, when other RPGs would point out we need the X to continue. The game really wants to hang its hat on comedy. There are funny tombstones and excessive references to classic lines in other video games. "Hey listen!" "Its a secret to everybody!" "Master of unlocking." "Welcome strangah! what-cha buyin" "I am error" "Motherbound" "Perhaps your prince is in another castle?" Even a reference to Bionic Commando that made me laugh, because that one was unexpected. The rest of the references have become commonplace on the Internet. Not only that, but there is a replica / parody of Zelda 2's version of Death Mountain. Other than that, the humor doesn't seem overwhelming. Sometimes less is more. I just didn't care for the game's humor like I did with Cthulhu Saves the World. Breath of Death VII feels like it doesn't have its own jokes and relies too much on your knowledge from 25 year old dialog. Then there are the game's other issues. Three years after its release, the game still has issues here and there. Enemies immune to poison, still get poisoned. Two dungeons have no music. That could be a good thing when all the other dungeons have the same music that overstays its welcome. Getting experience still seems glitched. plenty of times, I'd look at the status screen. I needed 4,000 more EXP, then beat another group of enemies earning 1,500 EXP only to discover that I still needed 4,000 more EXP. In a game where grinding is necessary, its an issue. I'm left with a feeling of knowing that I have to invest another hour into the game grinding before I'll face the boss of any area again. If you don't want to get too involved with a 40 - 80 hour RPG, Breath of Death could be for you. With saving anywhere and refilling your HP after every battle, that makes for an easy game. Some people like easy! Some complain that the game is 3 - 5 hours, that's perfect for $3 in my opinion. For the $1 combo pack that I bought it in. I feel like I got my money's worth thanks to hard mode. As for this being a fun, entertaining game, it wasn't. I spent several hours grinding to overcome boss after boss.  Maybe I made it too hard by playing hard mode and turned a 5 hour game into an 11 hour game with 6 hours of grinding, but I can only review my own experience with the game.

text: Honestly, I'm not entirely sure whether this or Spore has the title of the "Worst Case of Wasted Potential" in gaming history. But in order to make this review accessible instead of sounding like a pretentious skrub, I'll start with a general summary of the game (honestly, there is so little of a story anyways that spoilers don't even really exist) and then compare the good with the bad. Experience: I bought this game on 360 when it came out, had a blast, then forgot about it. So I rebought it a while back on PC after I had grown up and looked to see if it was how I remembered it was. The resulting dumpster fire was jarring, to say the least. The Gist of Things: -BRINK takes place on an enormous floating city called the Ark, which was an international project undertaken somewhere in the near future by all of the largest countries in order to provide a safe place for humans to take shelter and breed while the rest of the Earth was ravaged by some kind of ecological disaster (can't remember off the top of my head, because honestly the game spends so little on this cool premise in the first place that it doesn't remotely stick out). However, as they always manage to, society on the Ark sucks because the majority of the wealth on the island is concentrated in the hands of the few instead of evenly spread out (ala the French Revolution, even down to the percentages) and because of this there is an enormous amount of resentment from the underclasses (literally underclasses, since there's a giant tower in the middle of the Ark that extends like the phallus it is to screw over the workers) towards the high-rise dwelling scientists, politicians, and generally any semblance of law and order. Things get worse when riots start happening under the leadership of some really charismatic schmuck named Chen, who for all intents and purposes does absolutely nothing for his faction (uniquely called The Resistance) while his kinsmen commit domestic terrorist actions and generally stir up lots of trouble. On the opposite side there is The Security (another original name that ironically enough suffers from the same problems that The Security from RAGE did, in that it makes no sense for them to exist and they royally suck at their jobs, making me think that the writers of this game and RAGE alike had no originality when it came to things like this), led by a police officer/unelected president of the Ark named Mokoena. Naturally these two leaders (Chen and Mokoena) hate each other for no real reason at all other than plot magic, forcing the two factions of The Resistance and The Security to duke it out in objective gameplay matches. And I hope you liked that, cause that's basically the entire story, and that's not an exaggeration. The "campaign" (I use the term loosely because the campaign matches are copy-paste multiplayer maps with literally no difference between them) comprises The Resistance and The Security's continued efforts to become the most hated factions in all of fiction by doing nothing that makes any sense, such as The Resistance whining that nobody wants to join them after raiding and pillaging various Ark facilities, threatening (and then actually performing) a cruise missile attack on the giant tower in the middle of the Ark, and generally being rambunctious miscreants, while The Security furthers justifies this kind of nonsense by instituting martial law, unfair food/water rationing (even though everyone lives in a technological paradise because plot), and other such authoritarianism. Why should you care? You shouldn't, because this isn't even a game like Doom or Wolfenstein where the story is non-existent because it doesn't need to be. This game's story is a terrible excuse for writing and even though it had a decent if not good premise, the execution was something that honestly takes away from the experience instead of being just unremarkable (like other Bethesda titles one could name) Now that that wall of unreadable text is out of the way, let's get to the things you *should* care about. General Gameplay: BRINK is set up as a cooperative (i.e., not single player) FPS where the two teams fight each other while completing an objective (of varying nature) across a number of maps. You've seen it before in titles such as TF2 and Overwatch, and chances are you will regret ever thinking of those games while playing this one because you will hate your experience even more knowing how close this game was to being good. How BRINK differs from the traditional arena groove is its focus (or more accurately, attempted focus) on rapid and fluid movement, meaningful and responsive gunplay, and ridiculous amount of creativity and replayability due to the sheer amount of detail players get to play around with. There are three body types (Small, Medium, and Large) that affect the physical abilities and weapons you can carry, as well as four classes (Soldier, Medic, Engineer, Operative) that all have markedly different abilities. Now how well did that go? Keep reading and you'll see. The Good: -Amazing character creation, millions of combinations and they (mostly) work really well -The aesthetics of the game (because it definitely ain't realistic) are pretty good for 2011 standards -Parkour is fun and innovative, even if disorienting and the controls kinda suck -Level design is pretty good -I'll say it again, the level of detail in the character creation is really good considering this is an arena shooter where you don't even see said character very often -Music is kinda good I guess The Bad: -All characters in the game have an absurd amount of health and guns are generally useless at all distances other than point blank -Characters can be revived from LITERALLY ANY form of damage because magic -Unconscious characters (i.e., waiting to be revived) ALSO have way too much health and force the enemy team to spend time doing a finishing animation (nothing fancy, just a weapon butt) to kill them instead of wasting ammo -Ammo itself is very scarce because it takes 2 clips (that is not an exaggeration for certain ARs) to kill someone -Compared to character customization, gun customization is severely lacking -Given that there are about 8 maps (2 in DLC, iirc) and incredibly little variance between them, there is next to no replay value in this game whatsoever -Teams respawn in waves, so if you get sniped and nobody's around to revive you, you could be waiting up to *20* seconds to get back in the game -As mentioned earlier, the story is mostly absent from the game and when it is present it sucks -Most guns and their attachments can *only* be unlocked by finishing Challenges, which are tedious and easy-to-fail "activities" that exist solely to♥♥♥♥♥♥off the audience -The levelling system in this game is incredibly poor. You gain a level, you get a perk. However, most of the perks are uselss in the skill trees for the classes and because you are restricted to a max of 20 perks (for 20 levels) you have to play four seperate characters to be efficient (i.e., remotely competent) in any of the classes because multiclassing is discouraged. This is compounded by the fact that levelling takes a very long time and the grind is very tedious (grinding, in an FPS? Really?), as well as the missions being both unfun and quite long (playing defense can last 30-45 minutes per match if your team sucks). TL;DR: I would not recommend this game. However, if you look past its many flaws you might see something that could've been great if it hadn't made quite so many poor decisions. So if you actually decide to play this masochism simulator I would encourage you to play one character up to level 20, then uninstall the game and pretend you never experienced this.

title: broforce
text: Ok. So most positive reviews about this game are just jokes. This review is intended for those who want some actual info on the game. Broforce is a pixel-art shooter indie game that's main feature is the ability to play as a famous action movie hero. Each bro has a unique play style. Some of their weapons are similar, but still defer from one another. Their special abilities, which have a certaint amount of uses, are all unique and have varying effects. You fight terrorist, robots, aliens, zombies, and satan himself. The levels are well designed, and it's likely you'll get stuck on a few of them as the difficulty ramps up. Combat comes down to either an all out fire fight if you choose to charge in head on, or you can play stealthily and slowly work your way through the levels. Which technique you use heavily depends of the current bro you have. Extra lives are given when you rescue P.O.W.s and change to a new random bro. after so many rescues a new bro is unlocked. The gameplay is fast and chaotic and may be considered a con by some. Overall, and excellent idea with excellent execution.

title: brothers - a tale of two sons
text: First, the bad.  This game has no dialog, and I did not find that artistic, different, or at all engaging.  The lack of real language did not bring me "closer to the emotion" or any such thing.  It was just plain annoying and brought the level of the whole game down to a more cartoony, childish experience.  A little time spent on some sparse voice acting would have done wonders for Brothers.  I did not really develop an attachment to the characters, and without giving anything away let me say.. the ending scenes would have been much more effective at drawing out emotion if the two brothers were not so flat, and maybe a verbal que existed to tell me what the heck I was supposed to do.. Now, the good.  The scenes were very well done, and although a lot was left unexplained that is not necessarily a bad thing.  A richly detailed world fiction describing past battles and current world politics is something that would likely be ignored by most players (myself included) anyway.  Creating huge, dramatic scenes and leaving me to wonder what the heck is going on around the two brothers just made those scenes more interesting and drove my imagination.  Everything was beautiful to look at and the story was charming, at least what can be pieced together without dialog.  Level design was always interesting and I was never bored.  Some of the extra things you can do on the side were also pretty neat and unexpected.  I really liked the disparity between the two brothers' personalities, how they interact with things differently. I would not hesitate to pick this game up on sale.  I did, and I don't regret it.  However, if I had paid full price I would have been disappointed.

text: I won't say you HAVE to play this game, because I know when I hear people tell me that I automatically turn off. I will say playing this game was one of the best entertainment experiences I've had -- not just in gaming, but in any medium. I've played video games since the Commodore 64, but this one still presented me with so many things I'd never seen or experienced in a game before. The one I can mention in general terms without spoiling anything is the "emotional puzzle" near the end that integrates the player's use of the controller itself. You don't just need to solve a puzzle, but you have to have an epiphany about the story and the characters to "solve" it. It's brilliant.
